跟着在东京工作的ワン，从药局、牙医到119急救、地震台风、报案和心理咨询，学会遇: Follow Wang, who works in Tokyo, from the pharmacy and the dentist to calling 119, earthquakes and typhoons, reporting a crime to the police, and counseling. Learn to explain things clearly when something goes wrong, and not to be afraid to ask for help.
药局拿处方药: Picking up a prescription at the pharmacy
周四傍晚，ワン感冒发烧，在附近内科看完病，拿着医生开的处方笺走进诊所对面的「さく: It's Thursday evening. Wang has a cold and a fever. After seeing a doctor at a nearby internal medicine clinic, he takes the prescription the doctor wrote and walks into 「さくら薬局」, the pharmacy across from the clinic. It's his first time getting medicine in Japan. He doesn't know what an 「お薬手帳」 is, and he also wants to find out whether the medicine has any side effects.
社区药局的药剂师，五十岁左右，说话温和，记性特别好，常客的名字和药都记得: Pharmacist at a neighborhood pharmacy, around fifty; speaks gently and has a remarkable memory, remembering regular customers' names and medicines
在东京一家 IT 公司工作第二年的中国人，二十七岁，一个人住公寓，认真但不太会求: A 27-year-old from China in his second year at an IT company in Tokyo; lives alone in an apartment; conscientious, but not very good at asking for help
药剂师是专业人员，也是在为顾客服务，所以用「お持ちですか」「よろしいですか」这类: The pharmacist is a professional who is also serving a customer, so she uses courteous polite language and honorifics (sonkeigo) such as 「お持ちですか」 and 「よろしいですか」. Wang is the patient, so ordinary 「です・ます」 is enough; there's no need to force in complicated keigo. What matters is understanding what you hear and asking whenever you don't understand.
「お預かりします」字面是“替您保管”，药局、医院、银行接过你的东西时都这么说。听: 「お預かりします」 literally means "I'll keep this for you." Pharmacies, hospitals and banks all say it when they take something from you. When you hear it, just hand over your prescription (on your first visit, also your health insurance card or 「マイナ保険証」, the My Number Card used as an insurance card).
「お持ちですか」是「持っていますか」的尊敬说法，店员、医务人员对客人常用。自己回: 「お持ちですか」 is the honorific (sonkeigo) way of saying 「持っていますか」, often used by store and medical staff toward customers. When you answer about yourself, you can't say 「お持ちです」; say 「持っています」 or 「持っていません」. Honorifics are only used for the other person.
不好意思，我没有。那是什么？: Sorry, I don't have one. What is that?
不懂就直接问「それは何ですか」，一点也不丢人。药剂师最怕的是你装懂——药的事一旦: If you don't understand, just ask 「それは何ですか」. There's nothing embarrassing about it. What pharmacists fear most is you pretending to understand: once there's a misunderstanding about medicine, you're the one who gets hurt. If you're honest and say you don't know, they'll actually explain things to you even more carefully.
是记录你吃过哪些药的小本子。去别的医院时给医生看一下，会比较放心。: It's a notebook where we record the medicines you've taken. It's reassuring to be able to show it when you go to another hospital, too.
原来是这样。那请帮我办一本。: I see. Then please make one for me.
好的。您对药物或食物过敏吗？: Certainly. Do you have any allergies to medicines or foods?
用仿制药可以吗？会便宜一点。: Would a generic medicine be all right? It's a little cheaper.
「よろしいですか」是「いいですか」的礼貌版，服务的一方问客人意愿时用。「お安くな: 「よろしいですか」 is the polite version of 「いいですか」, used by the person providing a service to ask what the customer wants. 「お安くなります」 puts even the price in polite terms. All you need to answer is 「はい、それでお願いします」 (Yes, that one, please) or 「いいえ、元のお薬でお願いします」 (No, the original medicine, please).
那我给您说明一下。这是退烧和缓解嗓子疼的药。一天三次，饭后各吃一片。: Now, let me explain. This is medicine for your fever and sore throat. Please take one tablet three times a day, after meals.
「食後」一般指吃完饭后不久，「食前」是饭前，「食間」是两餐之间（不是“吃饭中间”: 「食後」 generally means shortly after you finish eating, 「食前」 means before a meal, and 「食間」 means between meals (not "in the middle of a meal"!). For the exact timing, go by the instructions on the medicine bag and what the pharmacist tells you, and if you didn't catch it, ask again.
饭后对吧。那个，有副作用吗？: After meals, right? Um, are there any side effects?
可能会犯困，吃完以后请不要开车、骑自行车。: It may make you drowsy, so please avoid driving a car or riding a bicycle after taking it.
明白了。如果有什么情况，可以打电话到这里吗？: I understand. If anything happens, may I call here?
当然可以。药袋上写着电话号码，随时打来吧。请多保重。: Of course. The phone number is written on the bag, so feel free to call anytime. Take care of yourself.
「お大事に」是对生病的人说的“多保重”，医生、药剂师、同事都会说。回一句「ありが: 「お大事に」 is the "take care of yourself" you say to someone who is sick. Doctors, pharmacists and coworkers all say it. Just reply 「ありがとうございます」. Be careful not to say it to someone who is healthy; it's only used when the other person isn't feeling well.
医生开的，拿到药局换药。「処方箋を出す」= 交处方笺；一般有有效期（多为四天内）: Written by a doctor; you take it to a pharmacy to get your medicine. 「処方箋を出す」 = to hand in a prescription. It usually has an expiration date (typically within four days), so don't leave it too long
能按处方配药的地方；只卖非处方药和日用品的叫「ドラッグストア」，有的药妆店里也设: A place that can fill prescriptions; a store that only sells over-the-counter medicines and daily necessities is a 「ドラッグストア」 (drugstore), though some drugstores also have a pharmacy counter
记录用药历史。看病、拿药、灾害时都有用，也有手机 App 版: A record of your medication history. Useful when seeing a doctor, when picking up medicine and in a disaster; there's also a smartphone app version
称呼时一般不叫职业名，直接说「すみません」搭话即可: You don't usually address someone by this job title; just start with 「すみません」 to get their attention
「副作用はありますか」「副作用が出る」。担心时直接问，不算失礼: 「副作用はありますか」 (Are there any side effects?), 「副作用が出る」 (to have side effects). If you're worried, just ask; it isn't rude
正式叫「ジェネリック医薬品」，成分相同、价格较低，可以自己选: The formal name is 「ジェネリック医薬品」. Same ingredients at a lower price; you can choose it yourself
相关：「食前」饭前、「食間」两餐之间、「寝る前」睡前: Related: 「食前」 before meals, 「食間」 between meals, 「寝る前」 before bed
「錠」数药片，胶囊用「カプセル」，药粉用「一包」: 「錠」 counts tablets; for capsules use 「カプセル」, and for powdered medicine use 「一包」 (one packet)
避免，节制: to avoid, to cut back on
比「やめる」委婉，医务人员常说「お酒は控えてください」: Softer than 「やめる」; medical staff often say 「お酒は控えてください」 (Please avoid alcohol)
「卵アレルギーがあります」「薬のアレルギーはありません」: 「卵アレルギーがあります」 (I have an egg allergy), 「薬のアレルギーはありません」 (I have no drug allergies)
现在多用マイナンバー卡当保险证（マイナ保険証），第一次去要出示: Nowadays the My Number Card is widely used as an insurance card (「マイナ保険証」); show it on your first visit
只对生病、受伤的人说，回答「ありがとうございます」: Said only to someone who is sick or injured; reply 「ありがとうございます」
服务的一方向客人确认东西时的标准问法，比「ありますか」更有礼貌，也比「持っていま: The standard way for service staff to check whether a customer has something. It's more polite than 「ありますか」 and softer than 「持っていますか」. You'll hear it everywhere: at pharmacies, hospitals, hotels and shops. Remember, this is what other people say to you. When you answer, use 「持っています」; don't use honorifics about yourself.
您带保险证了吗？: Do you have your health insurance card?
您有积分卡吗？: Do you have a point card?
动词辞书形／ない形 + ことがあります: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + ことがあります
用来说“不是一定，但有这种可能”。医务人员说副作用、风险时特别爱用，语气客观、不: Used to say "it doesn't always happen, but it can." Medical staff use it a lot when talking about side effects and risks; it sounds objective and isn't alarming. It looks very similar to 「〜たことがあります」 ("have done ... before"), but the meaning is completely different, so pay attention to whether the verb is in the dictionary form or the た-form.
有时会犯困。: It can sometimes make you drowsy.
有时会拉肚子。: It may sometimes give you loose stools.
动词て形 + もいいですか: Verb て-form + もいいですか
最基本、最安全的请求许可的说法。对药剂师、店员、邻居都能用。想更客气就说「〜ても: The most basic and safest way to ask permission. You can use it with pharmacists, store clerks and neighbors. To be more polite, say 「〜てもよろしいですか」. In Japan, if you ask before you do something, people will feel that you know how to respect their space and their rules.
可以用水送服吗？: May I take it with water?
第一次去药局、换了新的药、或者身体有过敏和别的病在吃药时，主动说出来、主动问用法: When it's your first time at a pharmacy, when you've been given a new medicine, or when you have allergies or take medicine for another condition, speak up without being asked, and ask how to take the medicine and about side effects. Answering these questions is exactly what pharmacists are there for.
不要药袋一拿就走，回家再上网乱查。也不要因为日语不好就一直点头说「はい」，结果连: Don't just take the medicine bag and leave, then go home and search around randomly online. And don't keep nodding and saying 「はい」 because your Japanese isn't good, only to end up not even knowing when 「食間」 is. Many learners take 「食間」 to mean "while eating," which is a classic misunderstanding.
药剂师听到你问「副作用はありますか」，只会觉得你是认真对待自己身体的人，不会嫌麻: When a pharmacist hears you ask 「副作用はありますか」, they'll only think you're someone who takes your health seriously; they won't find it a bother. It's actually people who ask nothing that worry them: did this person really understand?
日本的药局不只是“卖药的地方”。药剂师会核对你同时在吃的药会不会互相冲突，这就是: A pharmacy in Japan isn't just "a place that sells medicine." Pharmacists check whether the medicines you're taking at the same time might interact with each other, and that's what the お薬手帳 is for. One pharmacist I know greets her regular customers without even looking at their paperwork: 「〇〇さん、今日は咳のお薬ですね」 ("So-and-so, it's your cough medicine today, right?"). She even remembers if you mentioned last time that you can't stand bitter medicine. As she puts it, "When I remember their names, people feel they can tell me what's really going on." That kind of care is something we can learn from. The お薬手帳 can also be a lifesaver in a disaster: when a doctor at an evacuation shelter sees it, they know right away what medicines you normally take. So on your first visit to a pharmacy, go ahead and get one. If you don't understand, ask. Once everything is clear, the pharmacist can feel at ease too.
药剂师问你「お薬手帳はお持ちですか」，你没有，最合适的回答是？: The pharmacist asks you 「お薬手帳はお持ちですか」, and you don't have one. What's the best answer?
自己的事不用尊敬语，「お持ちではありません」是把敬语用在自己身上，不对。「大丈夫: You don't use honorifics about yourself; 「お持ちではありません」 applies keigo to yourself, which is wrong. 「大丈夫です」 is vague: the pharmacist can't tell whether you have one or don't need one.
药袋上写着「食間」，这是什么时候吃？: The medicine bag says 「食間」. When do you take it?
两餐之间（饭后约两小时）: Between meals (about two hours after eating)
「食間」指两餐之间，不是边吃饭边吃药。具体时间以药袋说明和药剂师的话为准，不清楚: 「食間」 means between meals, not taking the medicine while you eat. For the exact timing, go by the instructions on the bag and what the pharmacist says, and if anything is unclear, ask.
药剂师说「眠くなることがあります」，意思是？: The pharmacist says 「眠くなることがあります」. What does it mean?
有时会犯困: It may sometimes make you drowsy
一定会犯困: It will definitely make you drowsy
「辞书形 + ことがあります」表示“有这种可能”，不是一定会发生；「〜たことがあ: Dictionary form + 「ことがあります」 means "this can happen," not that it will definitely happen. It's 「〜たことがあります」 that means "have done ... before."
想知道能不能把药掰开吃，怎么问最自然？: You want to know whether you can split the tablet before taking it. What's the most natural way to ask?
请求许可用「〜てもいいですか」。「〜なさい」是命令；「いいよね？」对初次见面的药: To ask permission, use 「〜てもいいですか」. 「〜なさい」 is a command, and 「いいよね？」 is too casual for a pharmacist you're meeting for the first time.
